Until now, we’ve mainly used APL as a toolkit for array manipulation using its built-in primitives. Sure, it goes a long way, but to fully take advantage of it, we also need to be able to create our own functions and operators. Fortunately, the syntax -- if we can even call it that -- for user-defined functions, is super-simple. As someone said on the APL Orchard chat room, all you need to do is “slap curly braces around your code, and you’re done”. It’s not
that simple, but not too far off.

What if we need to modify multiple values? We could of course return an array of things, that’s a perfectly valid approach.

We’ve met some of APL’s built-in operators already, like
. Operators are perhaps the closest APL gets to the functional programming paradigm. An
is a function that returns a derived function. An operator can take other functions as its
operator that returns a derived function that can be called both monadically and dyadically:
2 (+/) ⍳10 ⍝ Parentheses not required, added for illustrative purposes
Here we see the monadic reduction operator, its sole operand being the plus function. The derived function it returns, plus-reduce, is called dyadically, with 2 to its left and
to its right. In this case, a windowed reduction. We could have said
to emphasize the fact that the operator really returns a function.
Dyalog lets us write our own operators, too, in a very similar way to how we write dfns. We call our own operators
. Operators can be powerful, but the need for them actually rarely arises in practice. The reason for this is that the built-in operators already let you apply your own functions in various ways.

This implements left-fold in terms of the standard right-fold by reversing the list and appending an accumulator element.
This version takes an optional left argument that can be used to initialise the accumulator:
Note the naming convention with a leading underscore for a monadic operator. This is just a stylistic choice making it easier to distinguish operators from functions.
Whilst there isn’t anything overly complex about writing your own operators as such, we probably won’t need to use many of them for the rest of this book, but at least now you have seen them.
